speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head K of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, I applaud the Ministry of Education (MOE) for the many changes it has made to better our education system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For such a time as this, when disruptions come fast and furious, we have no time to waste to ensure that our education system will, indeed, deliver the self-directed, self-motivated lifelong learners we need for not just a good economy, but also for a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What would our education system look like if we were designing it from scratch?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What are the sacred cows that should be examined, modified or slain, if no longer relevant?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to talk about five cows today, namely, Streaming, Gifted Education Programme, Competitions, the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) and Tuition.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Jack Neo, in his 2002 movie, "I Not Stupid", one of the highest-grossing local films, revolved around the lives of three students in the then EM3 academic stream, showing the ill-effects of labelling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, the negative effects of streaming were affirmed again by a 2018 social experiment video "Regardless of Class" hosted by Senior Minister of State, Dr Janil Puthucheary.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In it, youths from the Integrated Programme, Normal (Academic) and Normal (Technical) streams shared frankly, sometimes painfully, how they perceived each other due to the labelling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One good solution is Subject-based Banding (SBB) and MOE has done it and shown good results from it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not the first time that MOE has done away with streaming and labelling.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the point if academically gifted children only mix amongst themselves or with the academically strongest?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why do we not provide natural settings to let them interact and appreciate one another and other people unlike themselves?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For other subjects, such as Physical Education, Co-Curricular Activities (CCA), let the GEP candidates mix with their peers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It will make them better leaders and better human beings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The third sacred cow I ask for examination is the MOE's "best teacher/best student/best school" Competitions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the spirit of raising and celebrating as much excellence as possible, MOE should review the underlying principles and workings of the "Best Teacher", "Best School" and "Best Student" type of recognition schemes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we are aiming for every school, indeed, to be a good school in its own right and for as many excellent educators as possible, then these schemes should be reviewed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, there are so many great educators out there – more than 30,000 of them – and selecting one or a few of them as the best is not only a challenging task.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It does not do justice to the good work of MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us take reference from models, such as the Malcolm-Baldridge Quality Assuarance Schemes, which does not put a cap to the number of winners, but is a system that welcomes as many as possible who can meet the bar of excellence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on PSLE, the fourth sacred cow, which was delivered in 1960.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Abolishing PSLE will provide real space to provide students to become the curious, agile and more self-directed learners that the future economy needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Removing PSLE will also release some of the self-inflicted pressure and stress in students, families and teachers who have to choose between educating, learning or teaching to the test.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Removing PSLE will also remove a reason to feed the ever-growing tuition industry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are other ways of conducting formative and summative assessments at any age, in any interval.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government can carry out the change in a safe manner by allowing for a cluster of pilot schools with an opt-in option for those who believe that it is time for an alternate system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can refer to the best, such as the Yun-Ku school set up by Alibaba founder Jack Ma.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The tuition industry is more nimble and responsive to the needs of its customer base and MOE can learn from them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: MOE has started its own online learning platform to increase the access of good learning resources to all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thirty years ago, when I was an undergraduate, I worked as a relief teacher at Bukit Batok Secondary School.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I taught students from both the Normal and Express Streams and the students from both Express and Normal Streams were using the same textbook.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, certain segments of the textbook were not meant for the Normal stream students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a young and idealistic teacher at that time, I tried to interest the students in Science, no matter which streams they were from.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even when certain sections were not supposed to be taught to the Normal Stream students, I continued to teach them because I wanted to interest them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the Normal Stream students were quick to dismiss most of what was in their textbooks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They said, "We are taking the reduced syllabus, so no need to learn." There was a sense of resigned acceptance and defeat.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After the lesson, one Normal Stream student came to see me for advice.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She told me she had a deep interest in Chinese and she would like to study Chinese at the level that was the same as the Express Stream student.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I snapped at her and told her to work hard to get herself into the Express Stream.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, she would not have the chance to learn Chinese at the higher level.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Streaming has been a part of our education system since 1980.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It was introduced with good intentions, to allow every student to learn at a pace suited to their abilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Students in the Normal Stream often feel defeated and that limits their potential.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To address that, SBB was introduced, and it was very good.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, streaming of students into groups and bands has its advantages, both for students as well as for teachers.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Students can learn at a pace with others who are at the same stage of learning while teachers have to worry less about going too quickly for some students while going too slowly for others.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: However, streaming can have a negative impact and create a class-divide between those whom our education system deems to be academically able and those who are less so.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Over the years, we have seen the impact of streaming on students' self-esteem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Some students in the Normal Stream lose motivation over time, thinking that the label "Normal" means that they cannot excel or even improve.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We must recognise that our students' abilities, readiness and motivation can be developed and strengthened over time, and not everyone is cut out to excel at academic learning even if they are excellent in other non-academic areas.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Just because someone is not so good in class in certain subjects, it should not define them or lead to a loss of self-esteem.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In primary school, SBB has replaced the old EM1, EM2 and EM3 Streams since the mid 2000s.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: SBB now allows secondary school students from the Normal Stream to take certain subjects at a higher academic level.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Is it time for us to take the next step?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke about the immobility in our education system where a student who enters the Normal (Technical) Stream has little chance of leaving this stream.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke about how streaming can discourage some students.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How is MOE addressing the concerns of social stratification due to streaming?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of us may argue that streaming is necessary and helps to ensure that teaching can be pitched appropriately to students' learning aptitudes and at a pace suited to their academic abilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an academic, I can attest to that utilitarian purpose of academic streaming.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as a former secondary school teacher who taught students across the Express, N(A) and N(T) streams, I must also attest to the undesirable effects of academic streaming.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was a form teacher and a Mathematics teacher of a Secondary 3 to 4 Normal (T) class in 1999-2000.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I faced difficulty in getting my students to take an interest in Algebra or Trigonometry.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Between my cajoling and scolding, one of my students said to me in exasperation, "Cher, we cannot do Maths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not because they really could not do Mathematics, but because they believed they could not.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has served its purpose but it is time for us to move on and recognise that academic streaming places self-limiting beliefs on students who think they are only as good as the stream they are in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reality is that each of us has abilities and intelligences in different areas and to different extents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of us excel in languages, others excel in Mathematics or the Sciences, while others excel in Sports or the Arts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are still parents, employers and members of the public who believe that certain academic streams are inferior and will treat students from those streams with lower expectations, typical of what academics term the Pygmalion or Rosenthal Effect.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SBB already allows students to take different subjects according to their level of competency, and this is more than sufficient, without the unnecessary labelling.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see the day when a student's examination transcript and graduation certificate no longer indicate the academic stream that they were in, or if the student took the GCE "O" or "N" level examination.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, it will indicate the student took English and Mother Tongue languages at the Higher Level, Mathematics and Science at the Standard Level, or Humanities and the Arts at the Foundation Level, as an example.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see a student's examination transcript showing that the student has a diverse range of abilities in different subjects as well as their strengths in specific ones, and where you can, in no way, discriminate one student from another because of perceptions of their potential based on past abilities in high stakes examinations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are students who excel in Sports or the Arts but who may not excel in their academic studies because they do qualify for the Express Stream.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are unable to gain admission into the Sports School or SOTA.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With multiple options beyond secondary school, students who qualify for the Normal Stream should be allowed to be admitted to the Sports School or SOTA where they can still carry on their educational pursuits in the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), polytechnics or through other SkillsFuture (SSG)-related pathways thereafter.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot judge or limit a student's abilities in one area based solely on their abilities in another area because of current limitations in our admission criteria.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our current high-stakes examinations, such as the PSLE and the GCE "N", "O" and "A" level examinations, have led to an obsession with grades and scores, and the mistaken extrapolation of attainment to mean achievement and capabilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, there seems to be an over-reliance on tuition, sometimes guised as enrichment classes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some tuition centres implement rote learning and drill-and-practice methods to ensure their students can ace examinations, while other tuition centres have pre-admission tests to ensure only the most academically able students are admitted into their tuition programmes, further embellishing their tuition centre's track record.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, these tuition centres continue to charge premium fees for their apparent ability to produce examination top scorers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is of concern is that students from less affluent families will not be able to afford to learn some of these examination-acing techniques and will seemingly fall behind when examination results are used as a benchmark for achievement and capabilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the Ministry, this is a difficult matter to address.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The low-hanging fruits of economic growth would have mostly been picked by the time they are grown up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Innovation, yes, but what lies behind innovation is experimentation, trial and error, the discipline to reflect on our experience to learn and to do better, and better and better.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Aldous Huxley said, "Experience is not what happens to you, it is what you do with what happens to you".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That would be our young students' – and our country's – journey as adults.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In that journey, failure is a friend and teacher, not something that should be avoided at all costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lionising only success or people who are only successful may deter risk-taking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, in schools, published class rankings have been dropped, there are awards for most improved students, and participation in activities like competitions is recorded even if it did not lead to victory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more on two fronts to stoke the flames of resilience among our youths?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such stories do surface in the media from time to time, and some schools have been known to highlight students who have this profile.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But can we not entrench the showcasing of such examples of students as a regular practice in the cultural DNA of all schools?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only big global and national heroes but "everyday heroes".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can feed the rich tapestry of our children's imagination and give them hope to rise up from failures one day in their lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can help them learn that people may put you down today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But each of us should not only rise up from that but learn from that to become stronger, better people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, when junior colleges (JCs) are merged, one campus is picked over another as the site for the new merged college.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The rationale for some of these selections has been quite puzzling.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I hope the Minister can explain the rationale.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Also, many of the current JC buildings are old and dated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This introduced a lecture and tutorial system, akin to the university model, for students pursuing a two-year GCE "A" level course to gain entry into universities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fifty years later, this remains one of the most direct routes to universities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, the bulk of our JCs are more 30 years old.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over this period, the JC curriculum has been reviewed and enhanced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, in 2002, it was reported in this House that the curriculum was broadened to include Project Work to develop flexible thinking and a creative bent amongst our students.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may be an opportune time to consider whether the older JCs have adequate facilities to deal with the expanded curriculum requirements and desired educational outcomes for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What are the development plans that MOE has to ensure that older JC campuses are adequately resourced and conducive for their students and teachers?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, one of MOE’s biggest achievements, in my book, is the enhanced support of students with special educational needs (SEN) in the mainstream schools and IHLs, through the Allied Educator (AED) Scheme and the setting up of SEN support offices in IHLs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: As a volunteer, I have met many SEN professionals from primary to higher education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many are very dedicated and put their hearts into helping their students with SEN.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They are critical to ensure that our education system is an inclusive one.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There are, however, challenges faced in this relatively new education support space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: First, on the challenges in the mainstream primary and secondary schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: As much of the focus in mainstream schools is on completing the academic curriculum, important non-academic life skills required for students with SEN, like social relationship skills and daily independent living skills, are either not covered or placed as low priority.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: When these foundations are not set, deficits in such skills are highly likely to present themselves as problems in higher education or at work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The capacity of AEDs is also a challenge.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Besides capacity, there is a need to systematically raise the capability and the skills of AEDs as the range of needs is diverse covering various forms of disabilities requiring varying types and degree of support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Capability of educators in general, the teachers, is also a challenge.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: These teachers might generally have an awareness of special needs education but usually not skilled enough in mainstream schools to handle such cases.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Although a whole-school approach for SEN support is said to be adopted in the mainstream schools, the implementation leaves much room for improvement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The access to Specialist Support is also quite limited.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The challenges I shared in primary schools and secondary schools are multiplied in the higher institutions as the SEN support system is relatively new, and the IHLs tend to be more autonomous.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Not all of them view SEN to be of priority.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Some may even view it to be not integral to their mission.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There are now inconsistent support levels in different IHLs, with different processes depending on the vision, commitment and diligence of school leaders, faculty members and SEN officers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many of the faculty members see making a curriculum accessible as "additional work".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There is also the risk of low rate of disclosure for fear of stigmatisation by the students or being bypassed in course offerings, internships or employment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: First, adopt a system that ensures a structured whole-school, whole-institution approach with ownership and responsibility from school leaders to all educators, and faculty members to AEDs and Special Needs Officers (SNOs), to parents and students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Raise the capacity and recruit more AEDs and SNOs in each education institution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Raise capability by ensuring a skills-based training roadmap for all target groups to deepen their needed capabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This function should look at the sharing of resources and best practices across all the institutions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And most important of all, MOE should actively seek out schools and institutions which are inclusive and doing good work in this area.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Denise Phua, I am afraid you have to convey the rest of the points to the Minister of Education directly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: — and encourage more people to join this league.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Mr Chairman, our mainstream schools are generally inclusive and made up of students with diverse abilities and backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, we still have some mainstream schools that are specially catered for specific groups.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: While we understand the need for differentiated teaching and learning and ability-based pedagogies, we must strive to provide a more diverse and inclusive environment for our students to better reflect society at large.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Students with special needs are usually enrolled in Special Education (SPED) schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Can classrooms in our mainstream schools be made more friendly for students with special needs, such as having barrier-free access as well as more teaching tools and resources, to support students with visual or auditory challenges?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Can our curriculum also be revamped to allow for more hands-on learning and less pen-and-paper or drill-and-practice exercises, and with more outdoor learning incorporated in the main curriculum?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What this requires is for us to look at all our educational institutions, including ITEs, polytechnics and universities, particularly the ITEs, to see how we can get this group of students to integrate into the curriculum and develop themselves along the way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The teachers would need to understand the learning disabilities of the students and how they are to be taught differently, or these students may need some additional tools to enhance their learning environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The point is not everyone learns in the same way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are our educational institutions, such as ITEs, sufficiently prepared, not only from the infrastructure point, but equally important with the IHL and ITE teachers who are trained to engage these students?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How are our IHLs being prepared to take in these students, and do we ensure that internship for SEN students in the ITEs, for example, are sufficiently appropriate, so that they would not be disadvantaged when they go out into the market to seek opportunities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, last year, I met a resident whose son has SEN.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The young man had strong support from counsellors and teachers in his primary and secondary schools and did well to graduate to a polytechnic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the transition to the polytechnic was too drastic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same understanding and support from lecturers and administrators were lacking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems that SEN support has improved in primary and secondary schools, but there is a big jump when graduates go on to tertiary educational institutes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry should look into increasing the capabilities and authority of SEN support officers at polytechnics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SEN Support Office should be tasked to train and advise specific lecturers and staff members when there is an individual student with SEN enrolled in the department, so that support can be customised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SEN Support Office should also be consulted when there are incidents involving students with SEN.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Denise Phua, you can continue with your eight points.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Mr Chairman, SSG, the movement to transform Singaporeans to become self-directed lifelong learners is growing from strength to strength.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, unlike the vibrant SSG scene for the typical workforce, the lifelong learning outlook for persons with SEN is bleak.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The prognosis of students exiting from the SPED pathway is not optimistic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Official school years for SPED students now end at age 18 or 21.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, the reality is that the education of these students is not complete at the age of 18 or 21.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many of these students need to be schooled in literacy and numeracy or the mainstream academics that we know.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But they also need time throughout life to learn a host of skills that are often picked up more naturally by their typical peers – skills, such as self-management, home and community living, sexuality education and skills on how to navigate in a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world that is rapidly changing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If we address this lifelong learning need well in a systematic and systemic manner, more of these students will take on regular or part-time employment to address the challenges of the shrinking local workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Even if they do not work, they can lead better quality lives requiring lesser support from others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Tap on the special schools’ existing information and communications technology (ICT) and classroom facilities and teaching workforce to facilitate the required trainings with partners from the community and industries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Start with regular part-time courses on a weekly basis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Make these CET centres financially viable through a revenue mix of Government grants, donations and fees.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Third, start small with SPED school alumni members.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For a start, target alumni of special schools and their family caregivers, including domestic helpers, who can help reinforce learnings after training.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The cost of not training this population is going to be far higher than equipping them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Let us continue to train and equip them for life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the MOE Kindergarten (MK) Programme seeks to provide affordable preschool education and pilot teaching and learning resources focusing on holistic development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, a resident shared the concerns of sending her son to kindergarten as he suffered asthma and severe eczema.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the boy had difficulties attending kindergarten daily, she sought an alternative for the son to attend kindergarten a couple of days a week.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the rest of the week, she wanted to home-school her son using the materials that she hoped the kindergarten would share with her.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I helped her to contact the MKs which were very helpful and open to discussing with the mother the options.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the end, the resident decided to look for other options due to the distance to the nearest MK.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would MOE consider piloting a hybrid programme to cater to parents who wish to home-school their children part of the week?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MKs can provide resources for home-schooling as well as dedicated teacher's support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will make early childhood education accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, while the main responsibility of bringing up a child belongs to the parents, our schools and the community play important roles as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parenthood does not come with introduction manuals and I am sure parents will find the systematic approach helpful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that these guidelines have been well-received so far.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Guidelines for School-Home Partnership are not just for parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a guiding principle for schools, the community and other stakeholders as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am curious to know under this framework how collaborative partnerships between the community and the school will help them learn to be responsible and active citizens while building confidence in themselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister share details and examples of how the joint effort nurture character, impart core values and help them acquire skills outside the curriculum?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, how do these projects and programmes serve and meet the needs of the community?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Almost half of the teenagers polled in a local research attached negative labels to people with mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Fifty percent of mental health conditions develop in children aged 14 or below, according to global studies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister agrees in his response to my recent Parliamentary Question (PQ) that "mental health is an issue to be taken seriously".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Stigma poses a huge barrier to seeking help.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With greater awareness, more people are stepping forward to seek help.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health education plays a big role in re-scripting public narrative and understanding of mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our current vocabulary of mental health is heavily influenced by the medical model which can pathologise human experiences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Increasingly, we have been moving towards a recovery-oriented culture.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This demands a new language to be taught.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The recovery language and one anchored upon strengths and resilience must be learnt and permeate our vernacular.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health literacy is not a frivolity but a necessity, in the absence of which, we find rampant misconceptions that mental illness is “contagious,” “weakness”, and unfairly engage in victim-blaming.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With greater understanding and support, help-seeking need not be shrouded in secrecy or looked upon as being shameful.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more beyond the occasional assembly talks on mental health, optional enrichment classes on wellness and offers of counselling as interventions for behaviour modification, often construed as punishment by students.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We can teach the recovery language and encourage dialogue to dissolve stigma.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our children and youths can be the mental health first-aiders of every household.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Partnering social service agencies and mental health professionals in the curriculum curation and provision of mental health education in all schools must be the way forward.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Ministry plan to make mental health education accessible for all, whether students, teachers, administrators, parents and caregivers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Singapore is an ethnically diverse country, and bilingualism has been a cornerstone of our education system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From 200 years ago to Independence, our forefathers had settled and rooted here and brought with them their cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, youths are immersed in our highly connected, cosmopolitan city.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is inevitable that they become estranged from their own cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, having a strong command of our mother tongue is the key to better understand our culture and fortify our sense of identity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the rapid development of Asia, the ability to communicate in our mother tongue gives us competitive advantage and opens up new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the Chief Executive of Business China, I have seen that many of our companies are able to seize business opportunities because our people are effectively bilingual and bicultural.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is reflected in a popular saying amongst my Business China colleagues, "Bilingualism offers boundless opportunities." It is important that we continue in our efforts to cultivate bilingual and bicultural talents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What else is MOE doing to ensure that our students develop an appreciation of our mother tongue languages?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is important because a united Singapore is not only important to our future, but also to our sense of ourselves, of who we are and how we make our way in the world.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Can we take the opportunity to complement these efforts with an increased focus in our schools on teaching Bahasa Melayu to all our schoolchildren?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is our National Language and a language of the region in which we are rooted.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Can we help all our students attain some basic level of proficiency in our National Language?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This year, again, the Budget speaks of strategic plans for building a strong and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Year after year – and this is because teaching all our schoolchildren Bahasa Melayu speaks to many of our enduring values and hopes that Budgets try to address.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Learning Malay will be good for the cognitive and intellectual development of our children who learn it as a third language.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It will also protect and preserve our multiculturalism and promote national integration and a sense of identity.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I understand we currently have conversational third language programmes for Malay at the primary school level as Enrichment but not as part of the regular curriculum.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As learning languages is best done when young, could the Ministry look into making the conversational third language programme part of the syllabus for all our primary school students who do not otherwise learn Malay in school?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, included as part of the regular curriculum for every primary school student, but without the pressure of exams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My concern here is that this again might lead to social stratification if only students who do well in certain areas can pursue those CCAs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: A student who loves basketball and wants to pursue this interest should be allowed to, rather than be told that he or she is not good enough and should choose another interest to pursue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui, you have two cuts of four minutes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: CCAs allow our students to learn new skills, pursue their interests and passion.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They also make like‐minded friends from diverse backgrounds as they learn, play and grow together.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I recently met two boys who did Wushu in primary school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And a big factor behind their choice of their secondary school was that it offered Wushu as a CCA.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, upon their enrolment, the school decided to stop offering Wushu.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of the boys then tried to transfer to another school and also asked other schools in the neighbourhood who offer Wushu to allow him to join their Wushu CCA.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also sometimes hear from students that they did not get into a particular CCA because they did not have the prior background from their primary school days.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Other primary school students shared with me that their parents chose a less time-consuming CCA on their behalf so they can focus on their studies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If they decide that they have an interest in a sport later on in secondary school, they may not qualify without experience.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe there is scope for more flexibility in the organising of CCAs for our students.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In this way, we can use the expertise and resources of national-level sporting bodies and associations to conduct these CCAs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The combination of students within the geography will also allow for more social mixing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some students participate in activities outside of school on their own time, for example, football activities or training organised by the local grassroots Community Sports Clubs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Students who take their interest seriously often find that they do not know where to continue their interest after they graduate from secondary school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Having CCAs outside of school gives them a chance to continue their interest in community sports organisations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope MOE can work with the People's Association and Sport SG to develop some CCAs that can be pursued at the post‐secondary level.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I urge MOE to look into my suggestions so that we can help students enjoy a more enriching CCA experience.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Singapore is proud to be a clean and green city.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This concept extends beyond merely planting trees to being environmentally friendly, with many green initiatives ranging from green buildings to the 4Rs of Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Refuse.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Despite the various steps that have been taken so far, I believe that more can be done, especially on the part of individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our schools, especially, can play a big role by educating our students on the importance of green initiatives and the perils of global warming.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Make it part of compulsory curriculum as early as possible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Teach them what is recyclable, what is the correct way to recycle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Educate them on the Semakau landfills and incinerators.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Schools can teach our children to make green actions a habit and lifestyle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Take the lead in reducing the use of single-use plastics, such as straws and plastic bags.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Reuse textbooks by handing them down when students leave school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today's Straits Times also carries an article on water conservation camp.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Schools can organise camps, talks and activities on eco practices that involve parents and family members, so that such green habits can be extended beyond the school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are so many potential ideas that can be brainstormed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But most importantly, let our young understand what is happening to our planet, the perils of global warming, how our future generation will suffer the consequences more than the current generation, and allow them to explore and decide how they can all be a part of the solution.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, the Early Admission Exercise (EAE) was introduced as part of our efforts to reduce the emphasis on grades and focus on a more rounded education.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It was extended to the ITE last year, with no limits on the number of admissions by EAE.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It seems that students look on the EAE favourably.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, I would like to ask what is the MOE's experience with EAE?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Has it really been effective in helping students in finding their niches and in realising their aspirations?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are EAE students able to cope with the demands of the course work?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By this, I do not just mean academically, but do they find themselves enjoying it and wanting to learn more?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The other concern is that aptitude testing usually produces outcomes that are not as clear as an examination script.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But with aptitude testing, things like interviews, portfolios can be quite subjective.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And students will find more reasons to appeal against unsuccessful applications.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, according to a report last year, with EAE, polytechnic principals have been receiving more appeals from students and parents than before.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Has MOE done any survey on the challenges of implementing EAE?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What more can be done to recognise the students' interests and aspirations during admissions?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, one day, we can see aptitude testing replacing grade-based admission for our schools.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, over the years, we have done well to upgrade the standards of graduates from our ITEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Today, they are taking their place of pride in our workforce, and a good number are even making their presence in our other IHLs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The success is, in many ways, due to the way we brand the ITE and, of course, the level of competence of the graduates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The question I would like to raise is the opening of applications for ITE graduates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Currently they apply to the polytechnics after the GCE "O" level students have applied.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: ITE applicants can apply after the Joint Admissions Exercise for polytechnic and JC applicants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can MOE clarify on the JPAE and consider tweaking the process?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as a faculty member at an autonomous university (AU).

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because higher education is now accessible to all, we must ensure that every AU is a good AU.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are significant differences among AUs in prestige and resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These differences mean the more well-resourced AUs are able to spend more on faculty, teaching and research, even if they get the same Ministry tuition grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While this estimate includes non-student spending, annual expenditure per undergraduate ranges from about $38,000 at SIT to about $100,000 at NUS and SUTD.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consider Accountancy, which all AUs except SUTD offer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Graduate Employment Survey shows median gross earnings were similar across AUs at about $3,000 a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, Accountancy graduates of the more established AUs earn much more at the high end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot conclude from differences in earnings that the more established AUs provide greater advantages, because AUs differ in how they select students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, we should understand why the more resourced AUs are associated with higher earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But greater cooperation and resource-sharing could improve efficiency and equality of opportunity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, I suggest greater sharing of library resources across AUs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because knowledge is now so specialised, there is a ‘long tail’ of books, journals and databases needed for teaching and research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is wasteful for all AUs to stock the same materials and the less-resourced AUs will not stock them at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should study establishing a common tertiary electronic library and seamless interlibrary loan system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This can follow the model of the University of California (UC), which operates one library system across 10 UC campuses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I suggest the AUs offer greater flexibility for students to take courses across the different AUs, to make better use of our national experts and increase the breadth of course offerings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is very important for advanced undergraduate and graduate courses, because the right expertise may only be found in a few professors in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This will also help make education more stackable and flexible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What can we do to ensure "Every AU is a Good AU"?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Chairman, I understand that the ITE Work-Learn Technical Diploma has been popular.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The ITE Work-Learn Technical Diploma is successful mainly because of its partnership with the industry players providing structured on-the-job training.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thus, I would like to enquire whether MOE has any plan to expand the programme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thirdly, I would like to ask if SSG and WSG are prepared to partner private companies to train their workers at their workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Many established companies have training wings to train their own workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How could SSG and WSG partner these companies to not only train workers for their respective companies but also to train workers for the entire industry?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In this way, the two Statutory Boards can tap on the training resources of the private sector to reach out to more workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At the same time, it also allows the private companies to upgrade their training capabilities to better align with the common goal of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Sir, I would like to declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Wealth Management Institute, Nanyang Technological University (NTU), a CET provider.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If deployed well, it can offer meaningful support to workers to build deep capabilities that are relevant to their fast-evolving jobs and meet their career aspirations, including transition to a more attractive job or a different industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Since launching SSG five years ago, there is now significant awareness on the need for lifelong learning amongst our citizens.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Based on my own experience and observations of other countries’ efforts in CET, there are best practices that can be adopted to accelerate the impact of SSG even further, in order to turn it into a real competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even as we are cheered by this finding, the measurement of training outcomes remains difficult, as acknowledged by the CEO of SSG.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Hundreds of relatively small training providers, with uneven quality, have been accredited under SSG.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This makes it difficult to select the right training partner.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is not clear how trainers are qualified, nor how training content is curated to meet industry and job market developments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is also unclear how training is linked to the attainment of distinct quantifiable skills, career advancement and wage growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I often hear the frustration of residents, particularly those who have been retrenched, that their efforts to attend training courses are not commensurate with the recognition accorded by prospective employers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many would say to me, "I already go for many training courses but still cannot find a job".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many are at a loss as to how to structure their training programmes so that the courses will have a meaningful impact on their business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many smaller employers lack inhouse Learning and Development support and do not know where to begin to identify those training programmes best suited for their employees from amongst the very long, long list of SSG courses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This partnership should consist of key stakeholders within that industry, including the lead Government agency, union, trade associations and chambers (TACs), and representative companies and workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They could form an SSG Industry Committee (SIC) and be the authority to chart the skills and competencies required for current and future needs of the sector, including a certification framework that lays out systematic skills ladder for that sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Certification level against the skills ladder can serve to guide career progression in the sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The LTP’s appointment will be based on their depth of knowledge of the industry and their capability to develop and deliver very specific industry programmes, to be evaluated by SIC.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: LTPs can either be a Singapore IHL or private training provider and be selected through a competitive tender process.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To help the LTP develop strong capabilities and scale to serve its sector over the long term, they will have access to programme development grants to support the curation of customised programmes for the sector, according to a set of quality and price criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, support the LTP to develop scale, perhaps through preferential programme funding, to support their investment in deep training expertise and capabilities to deliver best-in-class training programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The LTPs should serve as the respective industries' centre of excellence for training and education, so that training may be concentrated amongst a few high-quality LTPs, whose capabilities and delivery are subject to close scrutiny by SIC and SSG.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies need to change their business processes and workers need to learn new skillsets.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that support must be given to companies and workers in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, MOE must facilitate the direct admission of adult learners into our polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could MOE share on the efforts to increase the provision of CET opportunities and, at the same time, recognising the skills and knowledge that adult learners have gained in their workplace?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: SSG is a national movement to provide Singaporeans with the opportunities to develop their fullest potential throughout life, regardless of their starting points.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It hopes to inculcate a mindset of continually striving towards greater excellence through knowledge, application and experience.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Regardless of which stage you are in life, a variety of resources has been developed and made available to help you attain mastery of skills.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could MOE provide an update on efforts to help employers deepen workplace training capabilities and promote lifelong learning among workers to sustain the momentum of the SSG movement?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a Professor at SUTD.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The SSG programme has systematically introduced adult learning into our education landscape and implanted the idea of lifelong learning in the minds of Singaporeans.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Member for Tanjong Pagar, Mr Melvin Yong, spoke last week about the issues of relevance and scope of courses, the often considerable costs involved and time investment needed that workers may be unable to spare.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I, too, have heard similar feedback from my former students and professional acquaintances.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask, how MOE measures the efficacy of SSG provisions in terms of meeting changing industry needs.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, what processes have we put in place to review the content and quality of courses and instructors in general but also to ensure that industry perspectives are taken into account?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It has been four years since SSG was first announced and implemented.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Since then, many programmes and initiatives have been introduced to help Singaporeans hone their work-related skills as well as lifeskills that help them stay active, relevant and carry on learning for life.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Can the Ministry share updates on the SSG movement that provide options for lifelong learning, as well as updates on the measures to streamline systems and regulatory processes for PEIs and other private organisations that form part of the overall SSG movement?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: This becomes more pronounced when children from underprivileged or low-income families do not have adequate family or social support and do not receive the necessary attention or love to help establish their sense of self-esteem, self-worth and the ability to trust others.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Where the family is not able to step up, the community has to step in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Within our mainstream schools, our after-school care provision and programmes and collaboration with community partners are some examples of how the community has to step in and help underprivileged or low-income families of our students.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, all these need to be well-coordinated with extensive interagency support.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: What are some plans in supporting underprivileged or low-income families of our students?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How will these plans help in minimising the gap with students from more affluent or privileged families?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: As a Member of Parliament, I have seen firsthand how education has the power to change families and I think it is extremely timely that this task force has been set up to ensure that we understand what keeps some students from the most disadvantaged backgrounds from benefiting from our education system.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: We have a world-class education system which is accessible to all Singaporeans and it is, therefore, vital to ensure that all our children, even those from poorer backgrounds, have a good start in life so that they can go on to maximise their potential and lead meaningful lives.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: This would ultimately benefit not only the students themselves but also their families, the community and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: It will provide a springboard for the next generation of Singaporeans to build on, but we must start somewhere.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: If any of these areas have already been identified, perhaps we can work on it immediately and not have to wait until the task force has completed its work and submitted its report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Over generations, our families have moved up the social ladder through their children's pursuit of education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This compares to two in 10 for the Merdeka Generation and one in 10 for the Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Notwithstanding our achievements, I think we all can agree that there is still a need to address why some of our children are underperforming and how we can help them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With the rapid rate of transformation of our world, if these children do not equip themselves with skills for the jobs of the future, their own future is likely to be bleak.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Each of these children, even though they, cumulatively, do not represent a big number, are not mere statistical digits that can be ignored.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Each one of them, if they are provided with adequate motivation and support to overcome challenges and uplift themselves, they will be, as Mr Charles Chong just said, add value to themselves, their families as well as Singapore and be part of our success story.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This must be our aim since we are focused on building an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have gathered that in some of these cases, it is, ironically, the parents who do not provide support for their children's education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These parents, by reason of their personal circumstances, may not have the requisite parenting skills or motivation to look after their children's needs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There could also be situations where the children’s homes are not conducive for learning.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I made the point previously that the current statutory levers do not provide for interventions where parents do not give their children reasonable support for their educational pursuits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, early intervention programmes like KidSTART may flounder on the rocks of parental non-cooperation, an issue I have raised in this Chamber before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My parents were teachers in neighbourhood primary schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I remember my mother’s stories about how some students would not turn up to school for days or weeks and how she would go to their homes to follow up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: She would tell us the stories of some of the families she met on those trips, who faced multiple challenges, usually linked to poverty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In Singapore, a 2015 media report, cited in Karyawan in June 2018, the magazine of the Association of Muslim Professionals, cited concern about the high absenteeism rates among students from low-income families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Absenteeism can snowball and lead to a vicious cycle of disengagement, lack of confidence and worsening educational performance downstream.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But this data does not appear to be published on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I suggest, echoing the call made in the Karyawan article, that we compile and regularly publish statistics on long-term and chronic absenteeism in schools so that, as a society, we can debate what more can be done to move the needle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Well over 1,000 students are affected by chronic absenteeism in secondary schools alone, not counting primary school and preschool.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Clearly, there is a need for coordinated social work interventions to address this problem among all levels of students, one that involves MOE and the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) working with schools and preschool centres as well as VWOs and non-governmental organisations.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui, you have two cuts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: He said he had quit school and was looking for a job.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: He asked me if he could go to Singapore Hotel Association Training and Education Centre (SHATEC) as he always wanted to be a chef.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Last year, I visited again and learnt the boy was now working at a handphone accessories shop.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I told him we will follow up again when he is older and see if we can find a tradesman to teach him a skill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: He is the only child of a blue-collar couple.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I had thought that was a one-off case until I met another resident, a girl who did not attend the first month of her new secondary school posting.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: She was afraid to as none of her classmates got posted to the same school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Her father said that unless we could get her into the school of her choice, she would not have to attend school. "She is a girl.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Even then, we were worried she could not cope after missing the first month of school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: After all, it could be quite intimidating to jump from four to eight subjects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Thankfully, the school helped her to settle in.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I was told the number of dropouts was small.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I believe it is so important to keep our young ones in school for them to continue learning, participate in new activities, mature in their thinking and explore their passion and interests.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Secondary education is an important stepping-stone for students in our education system as it positions them for their future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It is an important transition period from childhood to young adulthood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Schemes, such as the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme and the School Meals Programme, help to ease some of the financial burden faced by these children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, I believe that more can be done to ensure that all our children are given a good start in life.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: When I first went to Tampines, I regularly noticed primary and secondary students loitering at void decks, even after 10.00 pm.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Therefore, right after the General Elections, I started a free bowling clinic for Financial Assistance Scheme students during the school holidays to keep them engaged, pick up a new skill and interact with students from other schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Each session has over 100 children, including children with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Through the programme, I met a girl, Jess, not her real name, who is active, popular and bright but she was one of the 10 students in her school who had a tendency to self‐inflict harm.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: When I asked her principal what was the handing-over process of such cases to secondary school, she said they would inform the principal of the secondary school and they would try to engage the students.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: However, soon after, in Secondary 1, Jess was found smoking at the void deck by my volunteers and, despite our attempts to reach out to her and invite her back, she refused.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In my interactions with young people, they begin to discover their freedom and independence in secondary school and feel that they have grown up.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: But they may still be naïve and gullible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: I feel that more can be done to help children from disadvantaged backgrounds not fall into bad company at such a young age.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Children from such backgrounds face a variety of challenges growing up.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Their parents might also have to work shifts, long hours, or take on multiple jobs in order to meet the needs of the family.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: In such cases, the children have to spend most of their after‐school hours without adult supervision.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: They might not have the support they need to help them study effectively.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: For such children who face difficult circumstances at home, after‐school care becomes even more critical.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: A structured care environment outside of schooling hours is an important form of support which will enable children to develop good habits and routines from young.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: For many of these children, the challenging circumstances they face persist as they become teenagers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: It is thus important that we continue supporting them as they make the transition from primary to secondary school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Some of our secondary schools have begun running after‐school programmes to engage students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: There are several reasons that are attributed to a student's grade performance in his or her studies, such as learning ability and situational factors, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Some of these attributes are beyond one's control, whereas there are some which can be managed and enhanced.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Learning styles refer to differences in how people learn based on their preferences, strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The differences may pertain to various elements of the learning process, such as taking in, comprehending, memorising and recounting information.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Many observations suggest that the learning process is most effective when it is in line with our learning style preferences.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Some people may find that they have a dominant style of learning with far less use of the other styles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Others may find that they use different styles in different circumstances.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: There are also studies that suggest a person's learning style is correlated to his or her personality.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This programme can be conducted after school hours, maybe during remedial classes, for students who have not been performing well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Psychometric tests, such as Myers Briggs Type Indicator or C-Vat, for those non-performing students to find out their dominant learning styles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Through this identification process, students who have similar or near similar dominant styles of learning can be grouped together and be supported with remedial lessons using appropriate teaching methods that can fit their dominant learning styles.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe such targeted approach will be able to produce a more positive outcome in assisting our weak performing students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Saranya is a student at Yuhua Secondary School, staying in a 3-room flat in Jurong West.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, the family is receiving financial assistance from various Government agencies and she used to have low self-esteem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: On top of that, we arranged for her to attend free tuition as her school results were not very good.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Our volunteers run a monthly mentorship programme with the youths based on learning theme focus, such as building character, leadership, ownership, serving with heart and to excel.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The volunteers also brought her along with other students in the same scheme for outings, such as Kidzania, River Hongbao and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Eventually, she did well enough in her GCE "N" level examinations and is now studying for her GCE "O" level examinations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: It used to take a village to raise a child in the past, but now it takes a division to raise a child.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: JCSAS is one of the two programmes that we help children from challenging families in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Over the years, we realised that it is not enough to provide financial assistance to children from low-income families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: We are also blessed to have a team of dedicated volunteers who care for the students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, we cannot do all these in isolation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For the schools in Jurong Central, they are supportive and provide us with information on how the students are performing in school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This is because our grassroots leaders are sitting in the respective School Advisory Committees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: For schools that are not in Jurong Central, it is a challenge for us to obtain such information.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: They often cite the Personal Data Protection Act as a reason.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This will enable the schools to open up to us, sharing information about the students and have a more targeted and holistic approach to assist the students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: At the same time, we can reduce duplicated efforts and make the best use of our limited resources.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: It is our Government’s approach that to help vulnerable workers in a sustainable manner is by encouraging work, levelling up skills, and raising productivity and wages of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: This is based on the core premise that having a job is still the best welfare, and full employment is still the best protection for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: One of its objectives is also to incentivise older workers to join the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: The WIS payout that an eligible person receives depends on his age and income.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: In general, older employees or those with lower income receive higher payouts than younger employees or those with higher income.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: WIS can supplement a person’s income, it may not be necessary for the payout quantum to be differentiated based on age to encourage the older workers to work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Alternatively, the Government can consider increasing the cash payout to 80% without affecting the budget allocated.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: This would then help the workers to have a higher disposable income for their living expenses.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: How can we encourage lower-wage workers to stay employed?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I applaud the Government for working closely with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Measures to help low-wage workers must be seen in totality.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I sincerely welcome the enhanced WIS that would put more cash in the hands of these workers and help build up their CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Our Government has also been generous in providing subsidies under the Workfare Training Support to enable low-wage workers to upskill and pick up knowledge relevant to their work that could enhance their productivity and perhaps wages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Many low-wage workers are also being helped through the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: It is my fervent hope to see more industry associations coming forward to work together with NTUC as a tripartite initiative to develop a PWM for the industry.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Apart from improving wages, we should, as a society, aspire for our workers, including low-wage workers, to have jobs not only with decent wages, but also decent working conditions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: The Government’s support to make changes to the Employment Act and issuance of the various Tripartite Standard has also helped to make the working environment better for the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Requirements for every worker to be issued with payslips and employment contracts, guidelines on term contract workers and others have ensured our low-wage workers can be better protected from unscrupulous employers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Everyone in society has a role to play.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Employers and building owners should provide reasonable working conditions, especially proper rest areas, for their workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
