text: You and I can also play our part to treat our lower-wage workers with dignity, such as helping cleaners by returning our own trays and treating them with respect.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I would also like to know what other plans the Ministry has to further improve working conditions for our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: The Singapore Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) is a national credential system that trains, develops, assesses and certifies skills and competencies for the workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Training programmes developed under WSQ are based on skills and competencies validated by employers, unions and professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Most employers would then choose the WSQ modules which could be completed in the shortest possible time, which may not necessarily be the best module to equip workers with the relevant skills and competencies.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: While I am heartened by the introduction of the enhanced WIS, I wonder if PWM has scope to be extended to more sectors to benefit more lower-wage workers to have better wages and better career prospects.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Apart from improving wages, as a society, we should aspire for our lower-wage workers to have jobs not only with decent wages, but also decent working conditions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: One example of decent working condition is the provision of proper rest areas for lower-wage and outsourced workers, such as cleaners, security officers, food and beverage service staff, and dispatch riders.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Some may feel that requiring proper rest areas is a trivial request.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: But it is not so, not when you work mostly on your feet and the only time you get to sit and rest is during your lunch or tea breaks.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: The irony is that because these workers are mostly on their feet, it is somehow overlooked that they also need a place to sit and rest and experience some sense of well-being while at work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: These rest areas should be well-ventilated, well-lit and have proper tables and seats for the workers to have their meals and to rest.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Other than rest areas, there must be proper lockers where personal belongings can be stored safely while they work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: All in all, beyond decent wages and decent working conditions, every one of us has a role to play, including employers, in providing decent and more pleasant working conditions for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For instance, as fellow human beings, we can treat our lower-wage workers with dignity and respect and not treat them as invisible beings.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: We can also help make their lives a little bit easier with small acts of kindness and thoughtfulness, such as cleaning up after ourselves, disposing of our litter and not leaving our litter behind, or by returning our own trays at hawker centres or food courts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: As the saying by John Ruskin goes, "A little thought and a little kindness are worth more than a great deal of money."

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was heartening to see that the Fresh Start Housing Scheme was introduced in 2016.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This was designed to help second-time families to own a home.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Applicants include those who have been divorced or widowed, for example.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These homes were more affordable because they were on 45- to 65-year leases.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There were a number of conditions which were imposed on applicants.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, one of the applicants must have been in stable employment for 12 months.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And beyond the Fresh Start, what measures is the Ministry exploring to better support public rental households towards home ownership?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I know that some young residents have lived in a rental flat since they were a baby, grew up in the flat and until they get to secondary school, they still do not have a place to call home.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is quite concerning that some of these families appear to be stuck in a perpetual cycle of poverty, so much so that they cannot afford a home under the Fresh Start Housing Scheme, which is specifically designed to help families living in public rental flat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My heart also goes out to the elderly sick, who seem destined to spend their twilight years in a rental flat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Is keeping up with rent a challenge faced by long-time occupants of rental flats?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What more is the Ministry doing to support rental households towards home ownership?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He lives in a rental flat with his daughter, and he was sharing about how difficult it is to get employment.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But his daughter is doing well in school.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, we managed to get him employment and started him off somewhere.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A few years on, he is still living in a rental flat, but the good thing is that his daughter is doing well in school and will probably graduate soon.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He has told me that he is trying to have a proper home for her daughter and probably own a home of their own.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I suppose his way out of rental and, in this situation, will all depend on his daughter, through her education and through his daughter doing well in school.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But there are many who may not be in the same situation as him, where the children can be independent and make good through education.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: All of us know that owning a home is important.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One of our key pillars for Singapore's welfare model is family as the first line of support.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But for one reason or another, family members may not be able to care for one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If we do a rough typology of family and care, we have two lines – able and willing – and we see that they fall into four categories.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Able and willing – no problem and no business of the Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another group – unable and unwilling – is also beyond policy consideration.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A third group "able but unwilling", has traditionally been the concern for social policymaking.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This group has been subjected to a wide range of interventions, including counselling, means-testing for public service and, at the very last resort, legislation against neglect, such as the Maintenance of Parents' Act.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have seen over the years how, even when they are able, some children do not care for their parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, I would like to consider the fourth group – willing but unable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How can we better support this group who want to do more but have little?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This House recently debated over the Motion of CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As we do so, I am reminded of the case of one of my residents, a man I would call "S" and his younger brother.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As their parents have passed away, "S" is left to care for his brother who suffers from cerebral palsy and is also wheelchair-bound.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The expenses for the two of them is about $2,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr "S" has problems looking for a full-time job as he also has to look after his brother.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The domestic helpers that he manages to employ tend to leave after a couple of months.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Caregiving challenges, coupled with financial challenges, are such that the case management for Mr "S" and his brother requires a customised and personalised case management which the current policy does not appear to address adequately.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So much of caregiving currently also rests on domestic helpers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We talk about respite for caregivers, but these are mainly for family members and relatives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, much of the heavy lifting – quite literally, in the case of Mr S, because they would have to carry and bathe these elderly or immobile patients – and this is borne by domestic helpers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is especially true in light of our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And by 2030, we all know that one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As of 2004, there were already more than 210,000 caregivers in Singapore tending to the disabled, elderly, and physically and mentally ill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Currently, within Singapore, there are support groups, community programmes and services within the social service sector that are providing help and assistance to caregivers in tending to their beloved ones.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given the rising need for caregiving in Singapore, the Government has, in recent year, mobilised action to provide greater infrastructural and services support to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, we have a dilemma of long-term care in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For instance, while there is a demand for institutions and services to support long-term care, money and space for such institutions are both limited.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need, therefore, to provide greater support for this "willing but unable group" to allow as many Singaporeans as possible to be cared for and housed by their own families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This includes domestic helpers who live in the same house.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What can be done to ensure the same respite and welfare for these helpers?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, when we go to the Homes to visit some of these patients, we should also find time to speak with and interview the domestic helper.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another way is to touch base with them during their medical checkups.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We now have a compulsory medical examination for helpers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we also include a psychological examination for those who are caring for the elderly or the physically challenged?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many helpers may not be given their days off, with family citing that they pay them in lieu.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But money does not compensate for a day off from the day grind.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another group of Singaporeans facing challenges are those who stay in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: MSF had earlier announced the plan to set up social service hubs in and around rental precincts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How will this initiative better support families living in rental flats, and how can the community play a part?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do so, will, of course, require us to start at MOE.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we need also to remember that MSF has a large part to do, to ensure that Singaporeans who are less fortunate, people like my resident "S" and his brother are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a special group which holds a resource that no state intervention can substitute – the genuine love and care of a family member.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The book and subsequent commentaries suggest that the system today is a major contributor to why poor families cannot break out of poverty.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There seems to be widespread acknowledgement and acceptance that social inequality, including but not limited to income inequality, is a serious issue that we need to address as a society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But there does not seem to be agreement on the root cause and what policies, or actions, will actually maximise the chances to reducing income inequality.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: And overall, there seems to be a dearth of robust discussion on this.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Many views are advocated without strong basis or justification.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Government, too, does not seem to have directly responded to much of the discussion or the positions proposed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Much of the ensuing debate, save a few thoughtful pieces, has seemed to have consisted of different views being presented but without much substantiation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, some forum letters in the Straits Times said that, indeed, the problem must be the system and prevailing policies.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Others have said that the problem must be the low-earning individual or family itself.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Two opposing views that cannot be reconciled in the absence of constructive dialogue and discussion.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Speakers included Minister Desmond Lee, Senior Minister of State Maliki Osman, and the Executive Director of Promoting Alternatives to Violence (PAVE), Sudha Nair.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I understand PAVE was the organisation that worked directly with the families in the interim housing project.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This book seemed to suggest that the system is not in itself the problem and that individuals themselves can be deciders of their own fates.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, in his book, Prof David Chan seems to warn against reading without discernment, "Therefore, be careful and calm when you do all kinds of survey studies, when you read articles in social media or in the mainstream media poll reports, and even scientific surveys or ethnographic interviews.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, the data, findings, interpretations and conclusions are not as reliable or rigorous as they claim or appear to be." We have in the course of one year two books with two different positions, with many resounding expressions of support on both sides, and not much of a response from the Government, at least thus far, on a topic that is critical and important to us as a nation and society now and in the years ahead.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the best ways to mitigate this issue is giving more support to Singaporeans facing challenges.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: An integrated case management approach focused on development of the human capital, which I suggested in 2008 in this House, is even more relevant today.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Prime Minister Lee said that Singapore must not allow social stratification to harden.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Helping needy families with jobs, upgrading them and encouraging them to stay in employment will assist them to support their family members, especially their children, better.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to address holistically the many complex and intertwining problems that many such families face.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These are: financial difficulty, balancing low-paying jobs with family responsibilities, childcare facilities, housing and healthcare needs and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Children from such families face a greater challenge participating in the education process.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, we should assist in childcare, kindergarten, after-school care placement for them, as well as individual handholding approach and follow-up for those with more educational needs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of these children, especially the youths, may be at risk of falling into bad company.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How can MSF intervene early and better support these children and youths so that they can seize opportunities and achieve success?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Improvement of delivering assistance to those in need is core to helping this group.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Unless we have this good outreach, the intention and whatever good schemes there are, will be wasted.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to identify and reach out to those in need, even if it means incurring expenses in manpower to do so.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We can tap this information of those in need from data with SSOs, grassroots and VWO referrals, house-to-house visits and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many schemes available to help those in need, but they are mostly incomprehensible and untapped by this group.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In order to reap the desired outcome, MSF can coordinate and facilitate those in need to apply and to tap from the various schemes at a "one-stop service centre".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will ensure that such families will not fall through the cracks.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This would, in turn, contribute to our goal of pursuing a sustainable approach in helping lower-income Singaporeans becoming more upwardly mobile.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What are MSF’s plans to support Singaporeans from the low-income groups, to help individuals and families improve their circumstances?

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank members who spoke on MOE Kindergartens (MKs) and students with SEN for their encouragement, as we continue with our efforts to support these students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The MK curriculum resources are developed by MOE for trained MK educators to plan and carry out specific learning activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The curriculum nurtures children holistically, in a social setting, so that they are confident, demonstrate strong social skills and have a good foundation in literacy and numeracy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Partial use would not be optimal for the child.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, we would strongly encourage parents to send their child to the MKs daily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked if we intend to make preschool education compulsory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, almost all Singaporean children aged five to six are enrolled in preschool.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To further make preschool education compulsory for the early years may not cater to the different developmental needs of young children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Instead, we are taking a more targeted approach through KidSTART and other outreach efforts to reach out to the more disadvantaged groups and level up opportunities for all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where possible, we encourage students with SEN to attend mainstream schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, for students who require intensive specialised assistance, they will be better supported in SPED schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To encourage inclusivity, understanding and empathy between students with SEN and their peers, SPED schools have forged close partnerships with mainstream schools and organised activities to promote closer interaction and integration among their students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, Assumption English School, Assumption Pathway School, Fajar, Greenridge, Jurong and Zhenghua secondary schools, together with Rainbow Centre, a SPED school, have come together for a Visual Arts Collaboration programme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Last year, the students created a 3D artwork from recycled materials titled "Skyline of our Community".

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The students bonded over their shared love of Art and the collaboration enriched them in many ways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Within mainstream schools, students have opportunities for inclusive interactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Students have shared that they learn useful life lessons from their peers with SEN, such as resilience to overcome daily challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They also realised that it is important to be there for one another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was echoed by Benjamin Loh, a Primary 4 student from Nanyang Primary, who was assigned as a buddy to a classmate with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Benjamin said, "By being a buddy to a friend with special needs, I’ve learnt how to take care of people better than I used to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I’ve also learnt that he can't do some things, but he's really good at other things.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He is really good at Art and draws very well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: My advice to other kids who might be worried about having a classmate with special needs is, don’t worry!

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When they are frustrated or sad, tell them you’ll help them." For Benjamin and his classmates, learning together in the same classroom environment is beneficial in fostering healthy, inclusive interactions with one another, whatever their perceived differences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about the quality and accessibility of resources for students with SEN in mainstream schools and IHLs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As our education system develops to cater to a wider spectrum of students, the support and resources we provide have been improving in tandem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our mainstream schools have introduced infrastructure accommodations and teaching tools to support students with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These devices include Frequency Modulation equipment, Braille notebooks, computer systems with specialised features, talking calculators, voice synthesizers, customised furniture and specialised software.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: More importantly, we have a strong network of support to guide students with SEN in their educational journey, from enrolment to graduation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Across mainstream schools and IHLs, our staff provide an ecosystem of support for students with SEN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For instance, they work with parents and the previous school to better understand the student’s needs and facilitate smoother transitions in their educational journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In mainstream schools, we have our Allied Educators (Learning and Behavioural Support), or the AED(LBS), who have all undergone a customised National Institute of Education (NIE) Diploma programme in SPED.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They can also attend a range of in-service professional development modules and conferences to strengthen their knowledge of special needs support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In addition, a core group of teachers in all primary and secondary schools are equipped with deeper knowledge and skills in supporting students with special needs, through a Certificate level training in Special Needs at NIE.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are known as Teachers Trained in Special Needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While we will continue to recruit and train these school personnel with deeper experience and skills, one of their key roles is to equip all their colleagues to better support students with SEN and their families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This creates a network of support for our students.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Learning Support Specialists in ITE have at least a Diploma in SPED.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What happens next for students with SEN, after graduating from school?

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To prepare them for transition into the workforce, the IHLs work on building up their confidence and independence while still in school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This helps them develop strong coping and management skills for life and to take charge of their own learning needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Education and Career Guidance Counsellors and teachers work with the students to help them identify their strengths and find work-related opportunities that interest and suit them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Likewise, the IHLs collaborate closely with SG Enable and other VWOs to support persons with special needs through internship and mentoring programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The benefit of strong collaboration between schools and workplaces can be seen from the example of Rachael, a former student from Cerebral Palsy Alliance Singapore School.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She is hemiplegic and has weaker functions on the right side of her body.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Despite her special needs, Rachael is confident, hardworking and has a passion for helping others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These traits positioned Rachael for success, when she started her community-based work experience while at school.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Rachael was partnered with potential employers for month-long work attachments at various businesses, such as a supermarket, a laundry factory and a cafe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Her teachers and job coaches taught her to travel independently from her home to the various work locations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: She was also supported with customised, on-the-job training opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, Foreword Coffee, one of her employers, provided visuals and labels to help her remember steps to take for certain tasks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To accommodate her reduced motor skills, they provided Rachael with an electric whisk to stir drinks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We acknowledge the significant challenges that persons with special needs face in adult life, and the need for them to receive timely and relevant vocational and life skills training.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, MOE already has various incentives to enhance lifelong learning for persons with special needs, beyond the regular CET subsidies and support available to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to partner community stakeholders to support lifelong learning for persons with special needs, including those from SPED schools.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOE will continue to work closely with students, parents, community partners, Government agencies and employers to help students with SEN realise their full potential.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, being truly inclusive goes beyond what MOE or the Government can do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It also requires society at large – employers, peers and the community – to be part of this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Workplace colleagues also have a role to play in creating an environment that is welcoming and supportive of persons with special needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Most importantly, I would like to encourage all to look beyond disabilities and think more in terms of what their strengths and talents are.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: See them as people who – just like everyone else – have hopes, dreams and aspirations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Education (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We should accept them as they are, and include them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, the SSG movement seeks to build a nation of lifelong learners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To do so, we are working in partnership with IHLs, private training providers, employers and TACs, as well as workers and unions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, on increasing quality and industry-relevant training courses through IHLs and private training providers; second, on enabling business transformation through skills upgrading for workers; and third, on supporting individuals for lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Prof Lim Sun Sun that IHLs must continue to focus on teaching quality and ensure their courses are relevant to the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides getting feedback from students, IHLs work with business leaders to review course offerings and content and collaborate with industry partners on research and student projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With CET now forming part of their expanded mission, IHLs have significantly increased the range of high-quality CET programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will introduce more work-learn programmes with different modalities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The IHLs have also provided more SSG Series courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, we have about 1,300 courses across eight emerging and priority areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a challenging task, involving changes to the way they organise and conduct their courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I want to place on record my appreciation to the staff and management of the IHLs for their hard work and perseverance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also been working with our training providers to develop industry standards and expand overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SSG and Enterprise Singapore supported a pilot initiative by the Strategic Association of Professional Training-Consulting Organisation (SAPTCO) to develop and export training programmes referenced to WSQ standards, starting with India and Vietnam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will help our training providers to export their services to overseas markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: You do not have to be a member of SAPTCO to participate in the pilot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I encourage interested training providers to get in touch with SSG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about streamlining of regulations for PEIs and other private training providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want our regulations to be pro-business while maintaining quality training standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SSG is reviewing our rules to reduce compliance costs and make it more convenient for private training providers seeking different types of regulatory approvals and will be making some changes later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, to harmonise requirements and streamline processes for training providers offering WSQ and private education programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will simplify the licensing process for providers offering both types of courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A risk-based performance management system will replace the current Continuous Improvement Review process for WSQ-Approved Training Organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, to reduce the cost incurred by WSQ training providers to issue e-certificates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has been an ongoing effort since 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So far, we have reduced the certificate fee from $2.60 to $1.20.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SSG is trying to further reduce this fee through regulatory streamlining and process review, so that training providers can enjoy more cost savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Of course, I hope they pass this through to the students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng and Mr Lee Yi Shyan spoke about the need for pro-business regulations during the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) Committee of Supply (COS) segment earlier today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We believe that smart regulation is an important enabler for supporting innovation and entrepreneurship and will help our training companies to grow and export their services overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It can be one of Singapore's competitive advantages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we must not assume that smart regulation will automatically happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Ang Wei Neng that Government agencies must be open to feedback and listen to feedback from the industry, listen to proposals from the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked about involving employers in worker training, and promoting lifelong learning amongst workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As companies restructure and transform with technology, they should also build capabilities in their workers to help them move up the value chain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Using technology alone is not adequate if the workers are not trained to optimise these tools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we do it well, enterprise transformation should result in higher profits for the company and higher pay for our workers – a win-win outcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During MTI’s COS, I announced enhancements to the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The training subsidy will be provided via a PSG (SSG Training Subsidy).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is additional funding, above the existing training subsidies of up to 90%, to provide extra support for companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also want to reinforce the message that worker training and skills upgrading are critical elements for business transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Companies can use the training subsidy for training that is aligned with their industry's Skills Framework, to support business transformation and meet their training needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have asked MTI and MOE colleagues to keep the application process simple, so that more companies can benefit from PSG and the training subsidy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about efforts to deepen workplace learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Companies can work with the National Centre of Excellence for Workplace Learning (NACE) to develop structured training plans for workplace learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Gardenia, a company that makes bread, is one such company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Its workers operate on 24/7 shifts, 365 days a year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This makes it challenging for them to attend external training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By working with NACE to develop a workplace learning blueprint, Gardenia is looking to bring training to its workers within the factories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It has also implemented structured workplace training for production coordinators under work-learn programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many of them are small and medium enterprises, with more companies in the pipeline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to work with TACs and the companies, including ongoing collaborations to train workers for the wider industry, a point that Mr Ang Wei Neng made in his speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har made a key point that while employees upskill themselves, employers need to recognise these skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I urge employers to recognise and support skills-based hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These Frameworks are jointly developed by employers, industry associations, unions, Government agencies and training institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Employers can use these Frameworks to develop career maps, articulate job requirements, design training programmes and recognise skills for hiring and career progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har also suggested appointing lead training providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will take on board Ms Foo Mee Har’s additional suggestions as we study ways to further enhance the services provided by these centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To sustain a strong ecosystem of CETs, lifelong learning needs to be part of our cultural DNA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have made encouraging progress, with SSG benefiting about 465,000 Singaporeans through a wide range of programmes in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, 96% of approved SSG Credit claims are for work-related courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun asked about the efficacy of SSG programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been tracking the progress of SSG since its launch in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also encouraged to see positive training outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From a survey of 3,500 learners who attended work-related training in 2018, more than 80% said they were able to perform better at work six months after the training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do additional longitudinal studies to supplement these surveys as we know surveys do have their limitations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A recent study by MTI found that for individuals who were not in employment, WSQ training increased their likelihood of securing employment by up to 3.5 percentage points in the year after training.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Jeremy Fong is a literature and history student, but he also chose to pursue a Diploma in Business Management and take modular courses on mechanical engineering at ITE and PEIs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With developments in technology and markets, Fong's Engineering and Manufacturing Pte Ltd has gradually transformed its business.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Just as how Mr Fong has taken it upon himself to reskill, remain relevant and lead transformation in his business, he also applies the same philosophy to his employees.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He believes that transformation and training need to take place together in order to achieve the best outcome.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: (In English): To conclude, Sir, SSG is a journey that we must take together with our partners and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SSG is essential to our economic transformation, but it is more than a programme or an initiative.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is a movement to encourage lifelong learning and continuing education.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to nurture a passion for deepening skills and a curiosity for new knowledge.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What we want to achieve is for lifelong learning to spark a lifetime of joy in our people.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, it is almost 7.15 pm.
Head K (cont) –  , (proc text)]  .

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, my colleagues have spoken about the changes we are making in our education landscape to give all our students the best chance to reach their fullest potential and to support Singaporeans in lifelong learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Even as we make these bold moves, the Ministry of Education (MOE) will continue to invest in our strong fundamentals that have been critical to our success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Bilingualism is an integral part of our national identity, and our mother tongue languages (MTLs) are a cornerstone of the education system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A strong grounding in our MTLs will enable us to engage with the region more effectively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the same time, we want to help our students stay connected to their heritage and gain a deeper sense of rootedness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, please allow me to say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling mentioned yesterday, we cannot do this alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Support from the parents and family is extremely important.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, we have built in a daily life element into our primary school Chinese curriculum to involve family members in the activities and use Mandarin in their daily lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, by preparing a "sunshine breakfast" together, students and their family members can learn how to describe the cooking steps and the ingredients needed in Chinese.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This new curriculum has been well-received and we will continue to make improvements as we go along.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOE will continue to work with the various MTL promotion committees, as well as our media and community partners, to reinforce MTL learning and the use of our MTLs, both in schools and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: One example is the National Schools Xinyao Singing and Song-writing Competition.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The competition aims to ignite students’ interests in learning Chinese through Xinyao music.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Students are encouraged to draw inspiration from their Chinese lessons and incorporate them into their song-writing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOE's approach has always been a balanced one, which is, to make taking a third language optional.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We thus introduced Conversational Malay and Chinese in 2005, to allow interested students to learn these languages at an enjoyable pace.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For students who wish to gain a deeper understanding of Malay or Bahasa Indonesia, we have also introduced the Regional Studies Programme (RSP) for them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We note Mr Faisal Manap's suggestion to extend the RSP to include more languages, but we should take a calibrated approach as there are resource challenges in opening up more third languages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Notwithstanding this, there is definitely value in having students gain a deeper understanding of the culture and language of other ASEAN countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Students can do so through student exchange or immersion programmes, which are also available to students who are not enrolled in the RSP.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, in today's fast-changing world, MOE is committed to developing our students holistically to enable them to navigate the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Participation in co-curricular activities (CCAs) help our students grow in their character and develop their lifelong skills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: CCAs provide our students opportunities to discover their interests and talents, while picking up the ability to adapt, be resilient and overcome challenges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Louis Ng and Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about the allocation of CCA places.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: All CCAs are designed to provide students opportunities for growth and self-discovery.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: When allocating CCA places, all schools carefully consider the students’ interests and options within their available resources and facilities, as well as the CCAs' optimal size for meaningful engagement among the teachers, instructors and participants.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With these considerations and limitations, some CCAs are allocated based on the students' strengths, besides their interests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We understand the concerns behind the CCA selections and MOE is studying the current school-based CCA selection process for ways to improve and better support the potential of our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To support students in CCAs with few members, some schools have come together to pool resources through combined CCA sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Depending on the outcome of this pilot, we will explore offering this in other CCA areas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui also asked about environmental education in schools, which is key in our larger effort to develop students holistically so that they can become engaged citizens with a passion for the world around them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, as we continually seek to enhance our education pathways to build up the next generation, we hope that their learning journey will prepare them well for the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, our schools remain committed to preparing our children to learn for life, but we cannot do it alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We call on parents, industry and community partners to complement our efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To address Mr Gan Thiam Poh’s question, I will begin by speaking about MOE's partnership efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MOE launched these guidelines as, over time, the partnership between schools and parents has evolved into a broad range of practices and expectations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The guidelines serve to provide greater consistency of practice within and across schools, and many parents are supportive of them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Besides schools and parents, our community and industry partners also play a part in preparing our children for life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Project Mi was a values-in-action project organised by student leaders in Bukit Batok Secondary School that involved the collection and distribution of rice to low-income households.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: While student leaders from the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) mentored them in the project, the Bukit Batok Citizens Consultative Committee assisted in identifying the low-income households, and parents provided the manpower and transport required for the delivery of rice.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Through this partnership, students had the opportunity to meet community needs and become more confident, self-directed and responsible citizens.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Beyond being sound in values, our students will also need to be mentally strong and resilient to be well-prepared for the future.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition, we have introduced a training programme in schools which equips students to be peer supporters to help identify distress among their friends and be supportive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Through CCAs, outdoor camps and community service, opportunities are also provided to develop resilience and confidence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Nonetheless, mental health is a complex and multifaceted issue that is of global concern.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There is no single solution and, hence, a many-hands approach to addressing this is needed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Such an approach benefited Haisan, a Secondary 3 student from Northbrooks Secondary School.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Haisan was facing family challenges which affected him mentally and emotionally and this led him to skip school frequently.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Together, the school and the youth workers from the programme helped Haisan to process and manage his social and emotional stress, helping him become more confident, emotionally stronger and resilient.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Haisan has since developed positive relationships with his family, teachers and peers, and is now contributing actively in his school’s Dance CCA and special interest group, Music Circle.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, we need to recognise that the complexities of the world today mean that we cannot educate our children in silos.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is when we work together with mutual trust and respect that our children benefit most.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: When my son was in primary school, my wife and I encouraged him in his initial interest in debate.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Along the way, we had the pleasure of meeting his teachers who guided the teams, staying till late in school to train them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As parents, my wife and I would bring him out to dinner after training and competitions, or the occasional pep talk for motivation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It was never about the winning or losing of his debates but about the process of learning and the camaraderie built with his teammates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Neither did we nor he expect this journey to span eight years of debating, but the close support from teachers, coaches and the debating community, as well as family, helped him to tide over the tough times and relish in ones of joy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Today, he continues to share this joy by coming back to spar with his juniors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Chairman, developing our children's passions requires support and commitment from parents, schools and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It may not be for us to say where they shall find their passion but that is something solely for them to discover.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their cuts and I thank my colleagues for answering most of the questions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will now address the last set of questions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After my speech, there will be a joint segment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some Members of the House asked me yesterday why issues concerning housing and Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) are being posed to MOE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is because we have a joint segment where MOE, the Ministry of National Development (MND), the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and MSF will address the issues on Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT) and inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have been implementing significant changes to the education system over the past several years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is despite our system being very highly regarded around the world and producing good student outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In our current position, it is easy to feel complacent and tell ourselves, "Let us tinker at the edges", but that would be a mistake.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must keep evolving, adapting, to ensure the system is fit for the future and, where necessary, take bold steps.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where we can build new pathways, we will.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where appropriate, we will invest resources to improve our infrastructure for education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But at our advanced stage of development, the defining changes are about processes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the most complex because we dive into the source codes of the system, recognise tradeoffs, optimise them and even find ways to break out of them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, we have to balance between the joy of learning and the rigour of education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our students need proper paper qualifications to open doors to jobs, but they also need to pick up skills which they need to progress in life and in their careers, and these are not so easily credentialed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we are recalibrating the balance wherever necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this context, I will talk about the following today: first, a programme to further improve our education infrastructure; second, an update on the SkillsFuture (SSG) movement – Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat has spoken about this, and I will focus on how SSG has led to building of new pathways in our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs); and finally, I will talk about how we will introduce greater flexibility in our secondary school system to help develop every student's strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, infrastructure developments, specifically for junior colleges (JCs).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Murali Pillai asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Four pairs of JCs were merged this year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The transition was relatively smoothly, thanks to the tremendous efforts from all stakeholders – teachers, students, parents, alumni members and advisors on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They designed new uniforms and school crests, composed new school anthems, and held numerous activities to get students from the merged JCs to get to know one another better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Great effort was made to preserve the heritage of the component JCs that merged, including the adoption of merged names.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I congratulate the four merged JCs for starting a new chapter and wish them greater achievements ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOE will need to trouble them a bit more, and I seek their understanding because a few of the merged JCs were amongst the oldest Government JCs, with campuses that have gotten somewhat outdated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When choosing which JCs to start with, we considered several factors: the age of the JC, the state of its existing facilities and also the availability of holding sites while we build new campuses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also considered whether MOE would need time to engage stakeholders for co-funding arrangements, because that would apply to the Government-aided JCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once complete, it will move back to the existing site.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, in the West – and maybe this will address some of Mr Ang Wei Neng's questions yesterday – Jurong Pioneer JC, which is now located at the former Pioneer JC site.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once completed, Jurong Pioneer JC will move there.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We chose this permanent site for the merged JC because of its convenience and accessibility.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Mr Ang Wei Neng mentioned, it is near the Jurong Lake District and will be served by the future Jurong Region Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) Line.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, in the North, Anderson Serangoon JC, currently located at the former Anderson JC site.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Prior to the merger, both were old JCs, Anderson JC at 36 years old, Serangoon JC at 31 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After merger, we decided to locate the merged JC at the former Anderson JC site because it is next to Yio Chu Kang MRT station and its facilities can better accommodate the merged JCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The same consideration is still valid in deciding the future permanent site of Anderson Serangoon JC.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means that at some point in the next few years, we will need Anderson Serangoon JC to move temporarily back to the former Serangoon JC site and move back to the current site when the new campus is completed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we will plan the transition so as to minimise the hassle to students and staff.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Phase 1 will be completed by around 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are already planning for Phases 2 and 3 involving upgrading the fourth of the merged JCs, Tampines Meridian, and also Victoria JC and the older Government-aided JCs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The new premises will support the evolution of JC education, where lessons are now a lot more interactive and learning is more holistic.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, instead of just the classrooms we have today, we will have seminar rooms which are modular and flexible, to support more interactive pedagogies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will have facilities that encourage sports and CCAs, such as indoor sports halls which will be designed so that they can also be open for community use, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The JCs will have campuses that are fit for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next, I will give an update on new pathways in our IHLs, as part of the SSG movement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our objective is to have a more flexible system of education upgrading that is not overly dependent on past academic results but takes into account the varied strengths of our people to help develop and fulfil their potential in many different varied paths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about the progress of aptitude-based admissions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, admission systems are moving away from an over-emphasis on past academic grades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The National University of Singapore (NUS), for example, has recently announced that they are looking out for polytechnic students with entrepreneurial experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will involve interviews and the showing of portfolios.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In a similar vein, we introduced aptitude-based admissions at ITE and the polytechnics through what we call the Early Admission Exercise (EAE).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: EAE, since it was implemented, has sparked a host of education and career guidance activities in secondary schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Students now go through personality assessments, speak to industry practitioners and counsellors, and visit companies for their learning journeys, in order to discover their interests and strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a good thing because self-discovery is actually a very worthwhile investment of time and effort in secondary school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The IHLs will require candidates to not just declare their interests and passions but demonstrate them, through portfolios, activities outside of school, or showing that they have the knowledge of a particular subject that is outside of the education curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is inevitable that with EAE, the polytechnics will receive more appeals from applicants, which the polytechnics will have to evaluate objectively and independently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The rise in appeals is inevitable, because EAE involves qualitative judgement and assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We expect the final enrolment through EAE to stabilise at around 20% of the total polytechnic intake.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in response to Mr Zainal Sapari, with EAE well-established, this year, it will be expanded to working adults for the first time, with consideration given to their current and relevant work experience, and not just their previous school examination results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if current procedures for application to polytechnics disadvantages ITE students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The answer is no, because although ITE students apply after GCE "O" level students, they belong to separate queues, and each group has separate places set aside for them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The way we deliver higher education has also shifted, with new work-learn pathways that champion "learning by doing".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2017, we launched the ITE Work-Learn Technical Diploma.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These courses provide ITE graduates with a skills-based apprenticeship pathway to attain a diploma.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, ITE launched four inaugural programmes, and enrolled more than 100 students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in response to Mr Ang Wei Neng's question, yes, ITE will expand the programme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This year, ITE intends to launch another 10 programmes, and it is already planning even more programmes next year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The ITE Work-Learn Technical Diploma will become a major programme in ITE. "Learning by doing" is also championed by our polytechnics and universities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we have more than 100 SSG Earn-and-Learn Programmes, and these have collectively placed 3,300 trainees into various industries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our universities have launched a total of 16 SSG Work-Study Degree Programmes, admitting over 150 students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One of the work-learn programmes that I found especially meaningful was the one for social work at the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those in the social work industry are very proud of their profession, and so they require social workers to be degree holders.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, that impedes the career prospects of students who went to Nanyang Polytechnic (NYP) to do a Diploma in Social Work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of them go to NYP to do this diploma out of passion but, ironically, cannot be certified as social workers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS can do this because of its unique role as a university catering to working adults.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some years ago, I informed the former President of Singapore, the late Mr S R Nathan, that a few autonomous universities (AUs) were keen to name one of their faculty after him.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He said that if this was to be done, he would like it to be a faculty of Singapore Institute of Management University (UniSIM), the precursor to SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I asked him why, he said: "Because it is a university for someone like me." Today, we have the S R Nathan School of Human Development at SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To Assoc Prof Walter Theseira's question, MOE will certainly support all AUs and encourage sharing of resources, where practical.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When MOE says: "Every school is a good school", we do not mean that every school is the same, but that each has its own unique strengths, and is good in its own way.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And whether a school is good or not depends on how well it fits the student, not whether it is popular or branded or highly ranked.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leon Perera talked about the importance of cultivating resilience, and a "can-do" spirit in our young.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Dr Intan Mokhtar talked about moving away from an unhealthy tuition culture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How students, parents and teachers behave, what they focus on in education, are the result of deeply ingrained incentive structures in our labour market, education system and the way that our society recognises success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think we cannot tackle these cultural issues with another promotional campaign, adding new stories into our syllabus, or adding more to our curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We could do all that, but it would not fundamentally shift the underlying culture which is deeply ingrained.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Having said that, we are not helpless either.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the evolution of our education system, and the broadening and rebalancing of how we measure success, we can shift the current culture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And indeed, we are starting to see changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why we launched the Learn for Life Movement last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Movement is a holistic, comprehensive, multi-year plan to evolve our education system for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we have two movements today – Learn for Life for school education; SSG for lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are a few major thrusts under the Learn for Life Movement, and MOE has launched two of them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first is to balance rigour and joy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If learning is just stress and no joy, there will be little chance of sparking passion and self-motivation that drive lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why we are revamping the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) scoring system, introducing applied learning into schools, and cutting down on the examination load.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOE has established an interagency taskforce called UPLIFT led by Second Minister Indranee Rajah to tackle the challenge of inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She will talk about the work of UPLIFT later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will explain the third thrust, "One secondary education, many subject bands".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Members know, our secondary school system comprises three streams, namely, Express, Normal (Academic) or N(A), and Normal (Technical) or N(T).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Denise Phua, Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Charles Chong, Mr Louis Ng and Dr Intan Mokhtar have raised concerns about the streaming system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, I want to acknowledge Ms Denise Phua and Dr Intan Mokhtar, who have actually raised this concern for many years now.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This year, Mr Louis Ng joined the call.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
